sections.overview: The common moorhen is a medium-sized member of the rail family, widespread in Europe, Africa and Asia. It lives at the boundary between land and fresh water, using both vegetated shores and the water surface. The similar American common gallinule, Gallinula galeata, is a separate species; American records published under the old combined name do not describe its present range.
sections.identification: Adults are about 32–35 centimetres long, weigh roughly 250–400 grams and have a 50–55 centimetre wingspan. The back and wings are dark brown, contrasting with bluish-black underparts; white streaks mark the flanks. The red bill ends in a yellow tip, and the frontal shield is red. Greenish legs and white patches beneath the tail are conspicuous when the bird walks or flicks its tail. A coot instead has a white bill and forehead.
sections.habitat: Vegetated lake margins, ponds, marshes and rivers provide feeding places and shelter. The moorhen readily occupies park ponds and other small urban wetlands, as well as rural waters. Dense waterside plants let it withdraw from danger, although it also ventures into open spaces. Its nest may rest among floating plants, on a small island or in a tree above the water.
sections.diet: It is an omnivore, eating water plants, seeds, fruit and grasses as well as insects, snails, worms and small fish. Food is gathered both in water and on land: it picks items from the surface, dips its head to reach submerged food, or grazes and searches vegetation along the shore. This varied feeding strategy allows it to exploit the foods available locally rather than depend on a single kind of prey.
sections.behavior: During spring courtship, a male approaches a female with its bill dipped in the water; the partners may then nibble at each other’s feathers. Both build and fiercely defend the nest. When disturbed, a moorhen usually runs into nearby cover instead of immediately flying away. If it does fly locally, the flight is often short and laboured. Outside breeding, winter feeding groups can form, while northern populations move away from severe cold.
sections.reproduction: British nesting records indicate usually five to seven eggs, incubated by both parents for about 20–22 days, and commonly two broods in a season. The chicks hatch covered in down and already mobile. Mobility does not mean immediate independence: adults continue to feed them, and older siblings sometimes help. Flight develops at roughly eight weeks, much later than the chicks’ first movements around the nest.
sections.ecology: Family relationships can extend beyond a single brood. Some independent young from the first brood remain on their natal territory and feed younger siblings from a second brood. In a three-year study, adults with juvenile helpers reduced their own feeding effort, while the total feeding rate of the family remained similar. Such cooperation changes how care is shared between parents and offspring, rather than simply multiplying every chick’s food supply.
sections.conservation: The species is listed globally as Least Concern, but local trends need separate attention. In the United Kingdom it entered the Amber list of conservation concern in the 2021 assessment. BTO’s winter series shows a 25 percent decrease between 1998 and 2023; these counts include continental visitors as well as residents. Loss of wetlands can isolate local populations and increase their vulnerability, despite the species’ ability to use modified and urban environments.
